implementation_notes: JavaScript has no blocking receive outside Atomics.wait, so the classic loop is replaced rather than implemented: an async function performs one bounded pull, handles the batch, and reschedules itself with setTimeout - never setInterval, which fires again even while the previous poll is still running - while AbortController/AbortSignal.timeout() supplies the bounded wait and the shutdown path. Broker libraries keep the same structure (KafkaJS eachBatch pulls a batch whose server-side wait is maxWaitTimeInMs, with resolveOffset/commitOffsets as explicit acknowledgement), so the pattern survives with promises and an event-loop scheduler instead of a receiver thread.
pitfalls: setInterval schedules ticks independently of the work, so slow polls overlap and two consumers process the same channel concurrently; a self-rescheduling setTimeout chain keeps one poll in flight.
An unhandled rejection inside the awaited pull or handler silently ends the loop, so each iteration must catch its own failures and keep the abort path alive.
An AbortSignal created only for the sleep cannot cancel the poll itself; the same signal must be passed into the pull so shutdown interrupts the in-flight request.
